slides.title: Get started
slides.html:
Two patty-paper triangles with two sides and the included angle marked equal. Students slide, turn and flip one onto the other and narrate each move.

  • I can describe the three or four motions (translate, rotate, maybe reflect) that carry one triangle onto another when SAS holds.
  • I can decide whether a marked angle is included before I cite SAS.

geo.title: Get started
geo.body:
Two patty-paper triangles with two sides and the included angle marked equal. Students slide, turn and flip one onto the other and narrate each move.

  • I can describe the three or four motions (translate, rotate, maybe reflect) that carry one triangle onto another when SAS holds.
  • I can decide whether a marked angle is included before I cite SAS.

slides.title: The big idea
slides.html: SAS follows from the rigid-motion postulates (Unit 3), ruler and protractor uniqueness, and the definition of congruence.

geo.title: The big idea
geo.body: SAS follows from the rigid-motion postulates (Unit 3), ruler and protractor uniqueness, and the definition of congruence.

slides.title: Worked example
slides.html:
Why SAS works (based on the SAS picture, Jacobs p. 147).

Read the worked steps
StepReason
Slide triangle ABC so A lands on D.A translation. Rigid motions keep lengths and angles (Unit 3 postulates).
Turn it so ray AB lies along ray DE.A rotation about D.
Because AB = DE, point B lands exactly on E.Equal lengths along the same ray end at the same point.
If C and F are on different sides of line DE, flip across DE.A reflection puts C on the same side as F.
The angles at A and D are equal, so ray AC lies along ray DF. Because AC = DF, C lands on F.Equal angle, then equal length.
All three corners land on D, E, F, so triangle ABC ≅ triangle DEF.Definition of congruence by rigid motions. We did not use SSS or the triangle angle sum.

slides.title: Worked example
slides.html:
A midpoint proof.

Read the worked steps
StepReason
M is the midpoint of AD and of BC.Given.
AM = DM and BM = CM.Definition of midpoint.
Angle AMB ≅ angle DMC.Vertical angles are equal (Unit 2).
Triangle AMB ≅ triangle DMC.SAS.
AB = DC.Matching sides of congruent triangles. No parallel-line facts needed.

slides.title: Common mistake
slides.html:
Jordan calls angle B the included angle between AB and AC.

Try it on paper first, then reveal.

Find and fix the error

A student calls angle B the included angle for sides AB and AC. The included angle is where the two sides meet: angle BAC.

geo.title: Common mistake
geo.prompt: Jordan calls angle B the included angle between AB and AC.
geo.correction: A student calls angle B the included angle for sides AB and AC. The included angle is where the two sides meet: angle BAC.

slides.title: Practice 1
slides.html:
AB = DE = 6, AC = DF = 9, and angle A = angle D = 40 degrees. Are the triangles congruent?

Try it on paper first, then reveal.

Reveal solution

Yes, by SAS, because the 40 degree angle is between the two sides.

Reveal second check

The slide, turn, flip steps from Worked example 1 place every corner.

slides.title: Practice 2
slides.html:
Same sides, but now angle B = angle E. Can you use SAS?

Try it on paper first, then reveal.

Reveal solution

No. Angle B is not between AB and AC.

Reveal second check

Those two sides meet at A, not at B.

slides.title: Practice 3
slides.html:
In the midpoint example, AM = 3x + 1 and DM = 10. Find x.

Try it on paper first, then reveal.

Reveal solution

3x + 1 = 10, so x = 3.

Reveal second check

Plug in: 3(3) + 1 = 10.

slides.title: Check yourself
slides.html:
In SAS, why must the angle be the one between the two sides?

Try it on paper first, then reveal.

Reveal solution

The proof lines up ray AC along ray DF using the angle at the shared vertex A; an angle elsewhere does not control where C lands.

Reveal second check

Name the givens and the theorem or definition used.
